summary: Derived the data model the approved Counter plan requires: exactly one table, public.counter, holding the single global counter row (id integer pinned to 1 by a check constraint, value integer not null default 0, updated_at timestamptz not null default now()), with a primary key on id, no secondary indexes, RLS enabled, and one policy — counter_select_public for select using (true). No write policy is declared, so the table is default-deny for insert/update/delete, which is what makes the approved plan's single audited mutation path (the increment_counter() security-definer function added by task T1) the only way the value can change. No ownership column and no auth.users reference: the PRD's stack line and out-of-scope list both exclude auth, and the approved plan's decision log makes the counter global. The scaffold's public.items table is deliberately absent from this schema plan — it is demo scaffolding the approved plan drops in a forward migration, not part of the data model this app requires. Every policy expression here references only the built-in literal true and objects this same plan creates; nothing depends on a function or table a later task introduces. This step was read-only analysis; the workspace was not modified and no commands were run, so no check is claimed as passing.

decisions.title: One table, public.counter, holding a single global row
decisions.choice: The schema is exactly one table with three columns: id integer not null default 1, value integer not null default 0, updated_at timestamptz not null default now(). A primary key on id plus a check constraint counter_singleton (id = 1) makes more than one row structurally impossible.
decisions.rationale: The PRD names one entity, Counter, with a single integer attribute defaulting to 0, and the approved plan's decision log fixes it as a single global row pinned to id = 1. Enforcing the singleton in the database rather than in application code means the API tier's update ... where id = 1 can never silently target the wrong row, and no code path can create a second counter.
alternatives: A table with no id column and an application-level convention that only one row exists — nothing stops a second insert and the update has no stable key
One row per session or device cookie, which the approved plan rejected because the PRD names one Counter and no auth
An append-only events table counted on read, which is the history of changes the PRD excludes
consequences: Every visitor shares one number and sees other visitors' increments
pnpm db:reset always returns the app to value 0, which the plan's acceptance checks depend on
Adding a second counter later is a schema change, not a data change — consistent with the PRD's multiple-counters exclusion

decisions.title: id is integer, not smallint
decisions.choice: The id column is typed integer.
decisions.rationale: The schema-plan artifact format restricts column types to uuid, text, integer, numeric, boolean, timestamptz, date, and jsonb; smallint, which the approved plan's T1 deliverable names, cannot be expressed. For a table constrained to exactly one row whose id is always 1, integer and smallint are behaviourally identical and the storage difference is two bytes on one row.
alternatives: Blocking on the type-enum gap and returning no schema
Typing id as text or uuid to sidestep the enum, which would make the check constraint and the plan's where id = 1 predicate awkward for no benefit
consequences: The generated migration will read id integer rather than id smallint; T1's acceptance check (a service-role read returning one row with value 0) is unaffected
The regenerated database.types.ts types id as number either way

decisions.title: RLS read-only: one select policy and deliberately no write policy
decisions.choice: RLS is enabled with a single policy, counter_select_public, for select using (true). No insert, update, or delete policy is declared.
decisions.rationale: A table with RLS enabled and no matching policy denies the operation, so omitting write policies makes the table default-deny for every mutation while still allowing the page to read the value without a session. That is precisely the property the approved plan relies on: the only write path is the granted increment_counter() function, which structurally enforces the PRD's no-decrement and no-reset non-goals. Reading is open because the counter value is application state, not user data — there is no auth in this app and therefore no identity to scope a read to.
alternatives: Grant an update policy so the API tier can write the value directly — that lets any caller set an arbitrary value, including the decrement and reset the PRD excludes
Leave RLS disabled on the grounds that the table holds no user data — this violates the harness rule that every table declares RLS explicitly and removes the default-deny guarantee
Restrict select to authenticated, which would make the PRD's own acceptance sketch (open the page, see the count) impossible in an app with no accounts
consequences: Anyone who can reach the app can read the counter value; nothing sensitive is exposed because the row holds one integer
Any future mutation needs its own security-definer function and grant — there is no general write path to lean on

A missing or wrong grant on increment_counter() surfaces as a runtime permission error when the button is clicked, not as a build failure, which is why T1's acceptance check exercises the RPC with the anon key

decisions.title: No indexes beyond the primary key
decisions.rationale: The harness rule to index the owner column every policy filters on does not apply: the select policy is using (true) and filters on no column. The only lookup the app performs is by primary key on a one-row table, which the primary key's implicit unique index already serves.
alternatives: Index value or updated_at, which would cost writes on every increment and serve no query the plan describes
consequences: No index maintenance cost on the increment path
If a later requirement adds querying by updated_at, it needs its own index

decisions.title: No ownership column and no auth.users reference
decisions.choice: public.counter has no user_id column and no foreign key to auth.users.
decisions.rationale: The mission's default — reference auth.users for ownership columns rather than inventing a users table — presumes owned rows. This app has none. The PRD's stack line says No auth and its out-of-scope list repeats it, and PRD non-goals are binding, so the approved plan removes the entire auth surface. A user_id column would be permanently null, and a policy filtering on auth.uid() would deny every read in an app where auth.uid() is always null.
alternatives: Add a nullable user_id for future use — dead schema that invents a requirement the PRD excludes
Scope the counter per user, which requires the auth the PRD rules out
consequences: There is no per-user attribution for increments and no abuse control, which the approved plan already records as a risk
Introducing auth later means adding the column, backfilling, and rewriting the policy — an accepted cost of following the PRD

decisions.title: public.items is not part of this schema plan
decisions.choice: The scaffold's items table is omitted from the tables array rather than restated.
decisions.rationale: This artifact describes the data model the approved plan requires. items is turn-zero demo scaffolding that the baseline migration's own header says to replace in a forward migration, and the approved plan's T1 drops it along with its seeded rows. Restating it here would declare it as required schema and would also collide with the applied 20260726000000_rls_baseline.sql migration.
alternatives: Carry items forward as required schema, contradicting the approved plan
Express the drop in this artifact — the format has no representation for dropping a table
consequences: The generated schema-plan migration creates only public.counter and does not touch items
Dropping public.items and trimming supabase/seed.sql remain T1's responsibility; if T1 skips them, seed.sql still inserts demo users and items and the database keeps a table nothing reads

decisions.title: updated_at is kept; no value check constraint and no trigger
decisions.choice: updated_at timestamptz not null default now() is included, maintained by the increment statement itself. No check on value and no trigger are declared.
decisions.rationale: The approved plan's T1 deliverable names updated_at and writes it in the same statement as the increment (set value = value + 1, updated_at = now()), so a trigger would be redundant machinery for one write path. A check such as value >= 0 would guard against nothing reachable — the row starts at 0 and the only mutation adds 1 — and would be a constraint the PRD never asked for.
alternatives: Drop updated_at entirely as the smallest possible schema — it is cheap, already named by the approved plan, and answers when the value last moved without being a history of changes
Add a set_updated_at trigger, which introduces a function this artifact cannot express
Add check (value >= 0), which invents a rule the PRD does not state
consequences: updated_at is correct only as long as every writer sets it; today there is exactly one writer
The column is not a change history, so the PRD's history-of-changes exclusion is respected

assumptions: This artifact format expresses tables, columns, constraints, indexes, and RLS only. The approved plan's public.increment_counter() function, its revoke/grant statements, and the insert of the single counter row are therefore not part of the generated supabase/migrations/<timestamp>_schema_plan.sql. Per the Supabase conventions, implementation task T1 adds them in its own forward migration covering what the schema plan does not.

Policy target roles are not expressible in this format, so counter_select_public is created without a `to` clause and applies to public — which includes both anon and authenticated. That matches the approved plan's intent (select to anon and authenticated) and, because the app ships no auth, anon is the only role that will ever exercise it.
The default expressions are emitted as written SQL: 1 for id, 0 for value, now() for updated_at. now() is a Postgres built-in and needs no extension.

The counter is global — one row shared by every visitor — per the approved plan's decision log and its own open question to the operator. If the operator answers that it should be per visitor, this schema changes: id stops being a pinned singleton and gains a visitor-identifying key.

Anonymous read access to the counter value is acceptable because the value is application state rather than user data. The default-deny requirement is satisfied for writes by declaring no write policy.
The value column has no upper bound beyond the integer range; the PRD's acceptance sketch involves three clicks and no formatting requirement.
risks: The generated schema-plan migration creates the table but cannot insert the singleton row. Until T1's migration inserts it, a select on public.counter returns zero rows and the page has no value to render — an empty result, not an error, which is the failure mode most likely to be mistaken for a UI bug.

Likewise, this artifact cannot create increment_counter() or its grants. If T1 creates the table's companion migration incompletely, the app has a readable counter with no write path at all: the Increment button returns a permission or missing-function error at click time, not at build time.

The check constraint id = 1 combined with the default makes a second insert fail loudly rather than silently duplicating state. That is intended, but any implementation that reinserts the row on a non-reset database (for example an idempotent seed without on conflict do nothing) will error.

If the schema-plan runtime ever treats the tables array as the complete desired schema and drops anything unlisted, public.items would be dropped before supabase/seed.sql runs, and the untrimmed seed's insert into public.items would fail pnpm db:reset. The approved plan's T1 trims seed.sql in the same task that drops items; ordering matters.

A globally readable and globally incrementable counter can be advanced by anyone who can reach the app, including scripted calls. The PRD excludes auth and rate limiting, so no schema-level mitigation is in scope; the singleton pin and the +1-only mutation bound the damage to an inflated number.
updated_at has no trigger, so a future writer that forgets to set it leaves a stale timestamp. There is one writer today.

This step ran no SQL. The policy expression using (true) and the check expression id = 1 are simple enough to be certain of by inspection, but neither has been applied to a live database in this attempt.
nextActions: Implementation task T1 must add, in its own forward migration alongside the generated schema-plan migration: the insert of the single counter row (id 1, value 0), public.increment_counter() as language sql security definer with search_path set to '' and body `update public.counter set value = value + 1, updated_at = now() where id = 1 returning value`, `revoke execute on function public.increment_counter() from public` followed by grants to anon and authenticated, and `drop table public.items`.
Trim supabase/seed.sql in the same task, removing the two demo auth users, their identities, and the three items rows, so pnpm db:reset succeeds once items is dropped.
Regenerate apps/api/src/database.types.ts with pnpm db:types after the migrations apply, and confirm a second run leaves the file unmodified in git status.

Verify T1's stated acceptance check against the running stack: a service-role read of counter returns exactly one row with value 0; an anon POST to /rest/v1/rpc/increment_counter returns 1; an anon PATCH on /rest/v1/counter changes no row and a follow-up anon read still shows 1.

Operator: the approved plan's open question about whether the counter is global or per visitor is still unanswered. This schema commits to global. Answering it after the migration is applied means a forward migration to reshape the primary key, so answer it before T1 runs.
